facts.summary: Mississippi has no state minimum wage statute; the Legislature's stated intent is to implement the federal minimum wage, so the applicable rate is the federal $7.25 per hour.
facts.sourceAgency: Mississippi Secretary of State (official Mississippi Code portal)
facts.notes: Section 25-3-40 declares the Legislature's intent to implement the federal minimum wage. Full section text is available through the SOS-designated official Mississippi Code (LexisNexis). 2026 bills (e.g., HB 108) proposing a $10 state minimum wage were introduced but had not become law as of this check; verify current session status.

facts.summary: Mississippi has no state overtime or daily-overtime law and no state salary floor; the federal FLSA (1.5x after 40 hours/week, $684/week salary level) governs.
facts.notes: Mississippi Code Title 71 (Labor and Industry) contains no general private-sector wage-and-hour or overtime statute; there is no state daily-overtime rule and no higher state salary threshold. Confirmed against the official MDES publication of Title 71.

facts.value: no additional protected classes beyond federal
facts.summary: Mississippi has no comprehensive private-sector anti-discrimination statute and adds no protected classes beyond federal law; the only state provision (for state-service employees) mirrors the federal classes.
facts.notes: Section 25-9-149 prohibits discrimination in state service on the basis of race, color, religion, sex, national origin, age, or handicap only, and applies solely to state-government employment. Private employees rely on federal law (Title VII/ADA/ADEA). Verify exact section text via the official Mississippi Code.

facts.value: follows federal (no lower employer-size threshold; no state FEPA)
facts.summary: Mississippi has no state fair-employment-practices agency for private employers and no state coverage threshold lower than federal, so federal employer-size rules (Title VII 15+, ADEA 20+) apply.
facts.notes: Mississippi has no state civil-rights commission or FEPA covering private employers; the only anti-discrimination statute (§ 25-9-149) covers state-service employment. Private-sector coverage is governed entirely by federal thresholds.

facts.value: no state FEPA deadline; file with federal EEOC (180/300 days)
facts.summary: Because Mississippi has no state fair-employment-practices agency, there is no state discrimination-complaint filing deadline; charges are filed with the federal EEOC under the federal 180/300-day deadlines.
facts.citation: No Mississippi statute (federal EEOC process controls)
facts.notes: Mississippi is not a deferral (FEPA) state for private-sector discrimination; the standard federal EEOC deadline is 180 days (no state agency extends it to 300 in MS). Confirm current EEOC guidance for Mississippi.

facts.value: Mississippi Whistleblower Protection Act (public employees only)
facts.summary: Mississippi's whistleblower statute protects only public employees from reprisal for reporting improper governmental action to a state investigative body; there is no general private-sector whistleblower statute.
facts.notes: Sections 25-9-171 through 25-9-177 apply only to public/government employees who report to a state investigative body (Attorney General, State Auditor, Ethics Commission, PEER, legislative committees, or a district attorney). Private-sector retaliation relies on federal law or common-law public-policy claims. Verify exact section text via the official Mississippi Code.

facts.summary: Mississippi has no dedicated wage-claim statute of limitations; unpaid-wage claims are contract claims governed by the general three-year limitations period.
facts.citation: Miss. Code Ann. § 15-1-49 (and § 15-1-29 for unwritten contracts)
facts.sourceAgency: Mississippi Secretary of State (official Mississippi Code portal)
facts.notes: Section 15-1-49 sets a three-year catch-all limitations period for actions not otherwise specified; unwritten/employment contract claims fall under § 15-1-29 (three years). FLSA wage claims follow the federal 2-year (3-year willful) limit. Verify exact section text via the official Mississippi Code.

facts.summary: Mississippi has no statute setting a deadline for issuing a final paycheck after separation; final wages are generally paid on the next regular payday under federal FLSA practice.
facts.citation: No Mississippi statute (Title 71 has no final-pay provision)
facts.notes: Mississippi Code Title 71 contains no wage-payment-timing or final-paycheck statute for private employers; there is no state-mandated deadline. Confirmed against the official MDES publication of Title 71.

facts.summary: Mississippi has no state disability-accommodation or interactive-process statute for private employers beyond federal law; state-service employees are covered against 'handicap' discrimination under § 25-9-149.
facts.citation: Miss. Code Ann. § 25-9-149 (state service only); federal ADA otherwise
facts.notes: No Mississippi statute adds accommodation duties beyond the federal ADA for private employers. Section 25-9-149 lists 'handicap' as a protected basis but applies only to state-government employment. Verify exact section text via the official Mississippi Code.

discrimination.name: U.S. Equal Employment Opportunity Commission (EEOC) - Mississippi has no state FEPA; state-service employment matters go to the Mississippi State Personnel Board
